difficultyReason: The stimulus flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion embedded in a medical context: the arguer treats a condition sufficient for a diagnosis as if it were necessary, concluding that without the marker the disease is absent. Each answer choice is a dense mini-argument; distinguishing the precise conditional reversal from valid inferences, base-rate reversals, and correlation-causation flaws in the distractors demands careful structural analysis.
stimulus: Lyme disease invariably produces a characteristic bull's-eye skin rash in infected patients. Dr. Chen examined a patient complaining of fatigue and joint pain — both common Lyme disease symptoms — but found no bull's-eye rash. Dr. Chen therefore concluded that the patient does not have Lyme disease.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exposure to asbestos fibers always causes measurable scarring of lung tissue over time. A construction worker exposed to asbestos for decades was recently found to have no detectable lung scarring. The examining physician therefore concluded that the worker had not, in fact, been significantly exposed to asbestos.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients diagnosed with influenza report severe muscle aches. A patient visiting a clinic reports severe muscle aches. The attending physician therefore concluded that the patient probably has influenza.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Streptococcal throat infections are the leading cause of bacterial sore throats. A child presents with a severe sore throat. The pediatrician therefore concluded that the child probably has a streptococcal infection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who regularly take aspirin tend to have lower rates of heart disease. A patient has been taking aspirin daily for ten years. The cardiologist therefore concluded that the aspirin is the reason the patient has no heart disease.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin C deficiency always produces symptoms of scurvy in affected individuals. A sailor on a long voyage developed symptoms of scurvy. The ship's doctor therefore concluded that the sailor must be deficient in vitamin C.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats 'Lyme disease → bull's-eye rash' (a sufficient condition for the consequence) as 'no rash → no Lyme disease,' which is the fallacy of denying the antecedent / affirming the consequent in reverse — more precisely, it treats a necessary consequent of the disease as if its absence proves the disease is absent, when in fact the conditional only runs one way. Choice A replicates this exactly: 'asbestos exposure → lung scarring' is taken to mean 'no scarring → no asbestos exposure,' denying the antecedent with the same structure.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument takes 'asbestos exposure invariably causes scarring' and concludes from the absence of scarring that there was no exposure — the same move as Dr. Chen's: treating a sufficient condition for the effect as if it were necessary.
explanations.B: This is a base-rate reversal (most X have Y; this has Y; therefore probably X) — the Carpaccio flaw, not the conditional-reversal flaw of the stimulus.
explanations.C: Same trap as B: a frequency claim about the category is misapplied to an individual presenting with a symptom — base-rate reasoning error, not conditional reversal.
explanations.D: This is a correlation-causation flaw: the argument attributes lower heart disease to aspirin without ruling out confounds. The stimulus commits no causal inference error.
explanations.E: This is actually a valid inference (modus ponens): 'Vitamin C deficiency → scurvy symptoms; patient has scurvy symptoms' — wait, that would be affirming the consequent. However, closer reading shows the conclusion runs from symptoms to cause, making it a base-rate reversal in direction, not the same conditional-denial structure as the stimulus. Moreover, the stimulus concludes the disease is ABSENT from absence of the marker; E concludes the cause IS PRESENT from presence of the effect — a different directional flaw.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole compositional fallacy: a property true of each individual member of a group is attributed to the group as a collective unit. The answer choices are dense mini-arguments drawn from economics, biology, law, and history; several superficially resemble composition but commit different errors, and one valid analog tempts students who focus on topic rather than logical structure.
stimulus: Each musician in the Hargrove Jazz Ensemble is an extraordinarily talented improviser. Therefore, the Hargrove Jazz Ensemble as a whole must be an extraordinarily talented improvisational group.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each sentence in the contract between Holloway Industries and its suppliers is clearly and precisely worded. Therefore, the contract as a whole is a clear and precise document.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Donner legislative coalition is composed entirely of senators who individually favor lower corporate tax rates. Therefore, the coalition will probably vote as a bloc in favor of the proposed corporate tax reduction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every cell in a living organism requires oxygen to function. Therefore, a living organism requires oxygen to function.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most star players recruited for the Meridian City football team this season came from winning programs. Therefore, the Meridian City football team will probably have a winning season.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each brick used in the construction of the Aldgate Bridge is individually load-bearing. Therefore, the Aldgate Bridge as a whole is a load-bearing structure.

explanations.correct: The stimulus infers a collective group property (ensemble talent) from the distributed individual properties of its members (each musician is talented) — this is the compositional fallacy. The fallacy arises because ensemble improvisational talent requires coordination, chemistry, and collective responsiveness, properties that don't simply aggregate from individual talent. Choice B commits the same error: individual senators favor lower corporate taxes (individual property), so the coalition will vote as a bloc for the tax cut (collective political action) — overlooking that collective voting behavior depends on negotiation, leadership pressure, and coalition dynamics that are irreducible to individual preference.
explanations.A: This appears to be the compositional fallacy but is actually a valid inference in most standard contexts: a document whose every sentence is clear and precise is, by definition, a clear and precise document — clarity is an additive, sentence-level property. There is no gap between the part-property and the whole-property here.
explanations.B: Correct. Individual senators favoring lower taxes does not guarantee the coalition votes as a bloc — collective political behavior involves coordination and group dynamics not present in individual preferences. This matches the stimulus's compositional flaw exactly.
explanations.C: This is actually a valid inference: if every component of a system requires oxygen, the system requires oxygen. The property 'requires oxygen' does distribute straightforwardly from parts to whole — there is no fallacy.
explanations.D: This commits a base-rate/probability error (most recruits came from winning programs → team will win), not the compositional fallacy. It does not attribute a part-property to the whole; it makes a probabilistic prediction from a frequency claim.
explanations.E: Like choice A, this is a valid inference: 'load-bearing' as applied to the bridge as a whole follows straightforwardly if each of its structural components is load-bearing. The compositional fallacy requires a property that genuinely fails to transfer from parts to whole.
